title: Defining and registering tools
notes: A tool definition has three parts: a name, a description, and an input_schema that describes its arguments.
The description is a prompt: say what the tool does, when to use it, what input looks like and what it returns.
Registering a tool means passing the TOOLS list on every request and mapping each name to a Python function.

slides.title: Defining and registering tools
slides.sub: How the model learns what your tools are, and when to use each one
sentences: In the last lesson, Scout asked for a tool called get order, as if it already knew the tool existed.
It knew because you told it, with a tool definition.
In this lesson you will read one line by line, see why its description matters most, and connect it to real Python code.

slides.title: Anatomy of a tool definition

note.text: The model sees this definition on every request. It never sees your Python code.

sentences: Every tool definition is a small Python dictionary with three main parts.
A name, short and unique, with underscores between the words, such as get order.
A description, in plain English, of what the tool does, when to use it, and what it returns.
And an input schema, which describes the arguments the tool takes.
Each argument gets a type, and its own short description with an example.
Inside the schema, a required list says which arguments must always be filled in.
The model reads this definition with every request, but it never sees your Python code.

slides.title: get_order, written out
slides.lead: This is the definition Scout uses. It is plain data: a dictionary your code sends with each request.

rows.out: What the model writes when it asks

rows.code: "description": "Look up an Orbit order by its ID..."
rows.out: When to use it, and what comes back
One argument: text such as ORB-10482

aside.label: Looks familiar?
aside.text: input_schema is ordinary JSON Schema, the same format you used for structured outputs in Module 2.

sentences: Here is the get order definition, part by part.
The name is exactly what the model will write when it asks for this tool.
The description says to look up an Orbit order by its ID, and lists what comes back: status, items, carrier and tracking number.
Under properties there is one argument, the order ID, and its type is string.
The required list says the model must always provide it.
If the shape looks familiar, it should: the input schema is ordinary JSON Schema, just like your structured outputs in Module 2.

slides.title: The description is a prompt

left.label: Vague
points: No hint of when to use it

right.label: Clear
points: "Look up an Orbit order by its ID, like ORB-10482."
When: any question about one order
Scout picks it whenever it fits

sentences: Here is the part beginners skip: the description is a prompt.
The model chooses tools by reading their descriptions, just as it reads your system prompt.
A vague description like gets data tells it nothing: which data, and when?
Faced with that, Scout may reach for a search tool instead, or answer from memory.
A clear description names the job, shows the input with an example, and says when to use it.
It also says what comes back, so the model can tell whether the result will answer the question.
Most wrong tool choices are fixed here, in the description, not in the code.

slides.title: Writing a good tool description
slides.lead: Write it for a smart new colleague who has never seen your systems.

bullets.text: What it does, in one plain sentence
When to use it, and when not to
What the input looks like, with an example
What comes back, so the model can plan

aside.label: Watch for overlap
aside.text: Two tools with similar descriptions force the model to guess. Make each tool's job clearly different.

sentences: So what goes into a good description?
First, what the tool does, in one plain sentence.
Second, when to use it, and just as useful, when not to.
Third, what the input looks like, with an example, so the model sends the order ID in exactly the shape your code expects.
Fourth, what comes back, so the model knows what it will learn before it asks.
And watch for overlap: if two tools sound alike, the model has to guess, so make each job clearly different.

slides.title: Registering: from definition to function

note.text: The definition tells the model a tool exists. The mapping to a function makes it real.

sentences: Defining a tool is half the job; registering it is the other half.
First, put all your definitions in one list, which we call TOOLS.
Pass that list to messages create with the tools parameter, on every request.
When a tool request comes back, a small dispatcher function looks up the tool's name.
It finds the matching Python function and calls it with the model's arguments.
The definition tells the model the tool exists, and the mapping is what makes it real.

slides.title: The mapping, in code
slides.lead: A dictionary connects each tool name to the Python function that does the work.

rows.out: Each tool name points to a function
Called once for each tool request
The model learns what it may ask for

aside.label: Only what you list
aside.text: Only functions in your mapping can ever run. An unknown name is refused, not guessed at.

sentences: Here is the mapping in code, and it is short.
A dictionary links each tool name to the Python function that does the work.
A function called run tool takes the name and the input from the model's request.
It looks up the function and calls it, unpacking the input so each argument lands in the right place.
And the TOOLS list goes into every messages create call.
This is also a safety line: only functions in your mapping can ever run, and an unknown name is refused.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: A tool is a name, a description and an input_schema
The description is a prompt: what, when, input and output
Register by passing TOOLS and mapping names to functions
Wrong tool picked? Fix the description first

sentences: Let us pull it together.
A tool definition has a name, a description and an input schema.
The description is a prompt, so say what the tool does, when to use it, what it needs and what it returns.
Registering means passing the list on every request, and mapping each name to a Python function.
And when Scout picks the wrong tool, read the descriptions before you touch the code.
Next, you will build three useful tools: web search, a calculator and a file reader.

midQuiz.q: Which part of a tool definition does the model rely on most to decide when to call the tool?
options: The name of your Python function
The tool's position in the TOOLS list
midQuiz.explain: The model never sees your Python code. It chooses tools by reading their descriptions, which work like prompts.
midQuiz.hint: The model reads the definition, not your code. Which part is written in plain English?

midQuiz.q: When customers give an order number, Scout keeps calling a help-page search tool instead of get_order. What is the best first fix?
options: Rewrite get_order's description: what it does, when to use it, and an example ID
Delete the search tool so get_order is the only choice
Ask customers to write their order number twice
midQuiz.explain: Wrong tool choices usually come from vague or overlapping descriptions. Say clearly what get_order is for and when to use it.
midQuiz.hint: Where does the model learn what each tool is for?

endQuiz.q: What does registering a tool involve?
options: Uploading your Python function to Anthropic
Passing the definitions in the tools parameter, and mapping each name to a function in your code
Mentioning the tool's name somewhere in the system prompt
endQuiz.explain: The definitions go with every request so the model knows the tool; your dispatcher maps names to functions. Your code never leaves your machine.
endQuiz.hint: There are two halves: what the model sees, and what your code does.

endQuiz.q: get_order's input_schema lists order_id under required. What does that tell the model?
options: Every get_order call must include an order_id
It can leave order_id out if it isn't sure
Your code will invent an order_id when one is missing
endQuiz.explain: required lists the arguments every call must include. If the customer hasn't given an ID, a good agent asks for it before calling.
endQuiz.hint: What does the word required promise?
